newsitem.title: USA: Consumer spending slowed in September, incomes up.
newsitem.headline: Consumer spending slowed in September, incomes up.

text.p: Consumers spent frugally in September despite solid gains in incomes, the Commerce Department said Thursday, and socked more money into savings.

Spending rose a slim 0.1 percent, or $3.4 billion, to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $5.18 trillion after a 0.5 percent August gain. Incomes from wages, salaries and all other sources climbed 0.6 percent, or $41.5 billion, to a rate of $6.54 trillion after a 0.5 percent August rise.
The report further confirmed a pullback in spending during the third quarter that the government said played a major role in slowing the economy's rate of growth during the summer and early fall.

Savings jumped to 5.7 cents out of each dollar earned during September from 5.2 cents in August, the strongest savings rate in more than 2-1/2 years, since 6.3 cents per dollar earned was put into savings in December 1993.
On Wednesday, Commerce reported that national economic growth weakened sharply during the July-September third quarter to an annual rate of 2.2 percent, down from 4.7 percent in the second quarter.
A key reason for the slowdown was that spending by consumers was at a near standstill in the third quarter, Commerce said, though companies continued to invest briskly in new production equipment.
September's solid income growth was anticipated because a previously issued report on monthly employment showed weekly hours and average hourly earnings all increased during the month.

Gains in personal income, which includes wages and salaries as well as income from sources such as dividends, interest and businesses, are essential for funding consumer purchases, which fuel two-thirds of national economic activity.
Spending on durable goods, which includes cars, fell to an annual rate of $634.1 billion in September from $643.2 billion in August.
Carmakers previously reported that unit sales of new cars weakened in September after an August surge.
Spending on nondurable products rose to a rate of $1.55 trillion from $1.54 trillion in August, while spending for services was up a modest $6.1 billion in September to $2.99 trillion.
Personal savings in September were at an annual rate of $322.5 billion, up from $291.8 billion in August.
Private-sector wages and salaries increased $28.2 billion in September to an annual rate of $3.02 trillion after a $27.2 billion gain in August.
Payrolls of manufacturing companies barely gained to a rate of $680.3 billion in September from $680.2 billion in August.
